title: Conformal prediction for labelling and updating online models in the presence of concept drift in cybersecurity
research_question: Can conformal prediction supply sufficiently reliable pseudo-labels to update online cybersecurity classifiers when true labels are scarce and the data distribution undergoes concept drift?
methodology: The study evaluates Adaptive Hoeffding Tree, Adaptive Random Forest, and Logistic Regression online learners on three public cybersecurity datasets covering Android malware, network intrusion, and malicious IP detection. A chronological initial segment is used for training and conformal calibration, while later examples arrive as a stream; high-confidence and high-credibility conformal predictions can be used immediately as pseudo-labels, with varying proportions of delayed true labels also supplied. The authors vary class imbalance and label availability, estimate marginal and conditional drift with total-variation-based measures, and report F1, Matthews correlation coefficient, sensitivity, specificity, and non-parametric statistical tests.

key_findings.finding: Conformal pseudo-label updates improve online classification in a substantial subset of dataset-model-labeling configurations, but the gains are not consistent across all conditions.
On the malicious-IP dataset, Adaptive Random Forest with conformal updates shows statistically significant improvements across the reported metrics for all evaluated true-label proportions.
On CICIDS 2018, the conformal-update strategy is especially beneficial for Adaptive Random Forest and Logistic Regression in the reported comparisons.
The effect of conformal pseudo-labeling is model- and dataset-dependent, and some configurations obtain little benefit or deteriorate.
Larger concept drift is associated with smaller expected gains from the conformal-update mechanism in the authors' experiments.
Concept drift can make a previously calibrated conformal mechanism stale because the exchangeability conditions underlying conventional conformal validity no longer hold for the evolving stream.

limitations: Classical conformal validity relies on exchangeability, an assumption explicitly challenged by concept drift in the deployment stream.
The confidence and credibility thresholds used to accept pseudo-labels are experimentally chosen and can become inappropriate after distributional change.
The study covers three cybersecurity datasets and three online-learning algorithms, so conclusions may not transfer to other domains or model families.
Incorrect pseudo-labels can feed back into subsequent online updates and therefore propagate errors.
Improvements in F1 or MCC do not imply uniformly improved sensitivity and specificity; the paper reports inconsistent behavior for these operational metrics.
The experiments do not establish instance-wise selective-prediction guarantees after arbitrary non-stationary drift.
A public implementation repository was not identified in the paper material examined.
raw_claims: The proposed online update strategy uses conformal confidence and credibility to decide whether an unlabeled observation can be pseudo-labeled.
Only pseudo-labels passing high confidence and credibility thresholds are used for immediate model updates.
The experiments use three public cybersecurity datasets with chronological ordering.
The evaluated online learners are Adaptive Hoeffding Tree, Adaptive Random Forest, and Logistic Regression.
The study varies how many delayed ground-truth labels are eventually made available.
Evaluation includes F1, MCC, sensitivity, and specificity.
Conformal pseudo-labeling is beneficial in some but not all model and dataset configurations.
Adaptive Random Forest shows strong gains on the malicious-IP task.
Greater measured drift is associated with reduced improvement from conformal updating.
Concept drift weakens the exchangeability premise used by conventional conformal calibration.
